meta.title: Love Bombing
meta.subtitle: Recognize the Move Before It Owns You
meta.description: Twelve cards on how love bombing works, what it looks like in real time, and how to get your footing back before the hook sets.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: The Person Who Feels Too Good Too Fast
cards.hook: The early stages feel electric. But if someone seems perfect before they know you, that's the tell — not the feature.
cards.truth:
Love bombing works because it hits your brain the same way real love does, at first.
• The bomber gives you more attention than anyone has. It feels earned, not given.
• You feel seen and chosen. Your guard drops before you've decided to drop it.
• The trap: you're not being loved — you're being set up to need them.
cards.remember: If they're perfect before you've shown your flaws, something's off.
cards.theySee: A new partner who compliments everything, replies instantly, and acts completely fascinated by every word they say.

signals.t: They reply to every message within seconds, every time, from day one.
They agree with everything you say in the first two weeks — no friction, no pushback, ever.
They say they've never felt this way before you've been on five dates.
They present no flaws, no bad moods, and no complicated history in the first month.

steps.title: Write the timeline
steps.desc: List every big statement or gesture they've made and how many days you've known each other. If weeks one and two are packed — write that number down.

steps.title: Test their reaction to one small no
steps.desc: Decline one minor request today — dinner plans, a call, a favor. Note their exact response. Annoyance or guilt-trip is the data point you need.

steps.title: Share one real flaw on purpose
steps.desc: Tell them about a real failure or bad habit. Watch whether they absorb it honestly or brush past it and go back to telling you how great you are.

cards.script: "I like where this is going. I just move slower at the start — that works for me."
cards.counter:
When everything feels perfect and they keep pushing for more, the perfection is the tell.
• Notice: they fill every silence before you can think clearly.
• Say: 'I need a few days without talking — I'll reach back out.'
• Watch what happens when you go quiet for 48 hours. Calm is good. Panic is your answer.
cards.insight: Real intense attraction feels identical to love bombing at the start. The difference only shows when you slow down — and they won't let you.

cards.title: The Constant Message Flood
cards.hook: Texting you good morning, good night, and every hour in between isn't devotion — it's occupation. They're moving into your head before you've invited them in.
cards.truth:
Constant contact isn't about connection. It's about taking up all the space in your thinking.
• When they fill your phone all day, you start thinking about them constantly — by design.
• You feel attached before you've chosen to be. The attachment feels mutual. It isn't.
• The trap: when they go quiet, you'll chase. That's when control flips to them.
cards.remember: Constant messages aren't devotion. They're occupation.
cards.theySee: A person who texts them constantly from the first week, asking where they are, what they're doing, and what they're feeling.

signals.t: Good morning message arrives before you've woken up, every single day, from week one.
They ask why you didn't respond within minutes of opening their message.
Multiple messages arrive in one thread before you've responded to the first one.
They want a full rundown of your day every evening, by text or call, without fail.

steps.title: Count the messages today
steps.desc: Look at the last three days of conversation. If they sent more than 20 unsolicited messages per day, write that number down as a fact, not a feeling.

steps.title: Add a real delay now
steps.desc: Wait 3–4 hours before responding to their next message. Say nothing about the delay. Note exactly whether they panic, send more messages, or ask what's wrong.

steps.title: Set one hard window today
steps.desc: Pick one two-hour block in the next 24 hours where you will not respond to anyone. Tell no one about it. If they make that silence into a problem, you have your answer.

cards.script: "I don't check my phone constantly — I'll get back to you when I can."
cards.counter:
If someone you just met is messaging at this pace, you are already being conditioned before you've noticed it.
• Notice: you feel anxious when they go quiet, even briefly — that's the conditioning working.
• Reply slower, say nothing about it, and watch if they get tense or demand an explanation.
• If they push back hard on the delay, the message flood was never about connection.
cards.insight: Once you feel anxious when they stop texting, the conditioning already worked. The question is whether you catch it before anxious becomes your baseline with them.

cards.title: The Pedestal Problem: Too Many Compliments Too Soon
cards.hook: "I've never met anyone like you" in week one means they don't know you yet. That's not a compliment — it's a script they use before the real you shows up.
cards.truth:
Putting you on a pedestal early has nothing to do with how great you are.
• The bomber says extraordinary things before they know ordinary things about you.
• You feel uniquely seen. The feeling is real. The knowledge behind the compliment isn't.
• The trap: once you're on the pedestal, you'll work hard not to fall off it.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 32 — Play to People's Fantasies
cards.remember: Big compliments before real knowledge are a move, not a feeling.
cards.theySee: A date who says things like 'you're my destiny' or 'I've been waiting for someone exactly like you' before the third meeting.

signals.t: They use words like 'fate', 'meant to be', or 'I've been waiting for you' without irony.
They tell you you're completely different from everyone they've ever dated, unprompted, in week one.
They say you haven't done a single thing wrong, ever, in the first two weeks of knowing you.
They post about you or introduce you as someone special before you've agreed on what you are.

steps.title: List what they actually know
steps.desc: Write down five real facts they know about you — not your looks or your energy, actual facts. If the list is short, so is their knowledge of the person they're calling amazing.

steps.title: Share one real imperfection today
steps.desc: Tell them about a genuine failure, flaw, or bad habit. Watch whether they sit with it or brush past it and go straight back to telling you how perfect you are.

steps.title: Push back on one compliment
steps.desc: Lightly question one big thing they say today — 'I'm not sure I've earned that yet.' If they get hurt or push harder, the compliment was always for them, not you.

cards.script: "That's a big thing to say about someone you've just met. Tell me something real you've learned about me."
cards.counter:
You're being pedestalled when praise arrives faster than knowledge can justify it.
• Notice: they compliment your personality before they've seen it tested once.
• Say: 'I'm not sure I've earned that yet' — and watch what they do with the pushback.
• If they insist anyway, the compliment is about keeping you hooked, not about you.
cards.insight: The pedestal is comfortable right up until they decide you've fallen off it. The same person who called you destiny will say you've changed — and mean it.

cards.title: Future-Talk Before You've Had One Hard Conversation
cards.hook: If they're talking about moving in together before you've had your first real disagreement, they're not planning — they're anchoring you to something you haven't chosen yet.
cards.truth:
Premature future-talk is a control move dressed as commitment.
• It creates a shared story you'd feel you were destroying if you slowed down.
• You start thinking of yourself as part of a unit before you've decided to be one.
• The trap: walking away later feels like leaving something you already built together.
cards.remember: Future plans before real fights are a trap, not a promise.
cards.theySee: A new partner who has already named what city they'll live in together or discussed kids' names, on the second or third date.

signals.t: They bring up living together before you've slept over twice.
They plan or book a vacation months out with you before you've agreed on what you even are.
They bring up meeting their parents or siblings before two weeks in, as a concrete plan.
They raise marriage or kids in the first month as a serious, not hypothetical, topic.

steps.title: Name the pace once, clearly
steps.desc: Say: 'I want to get to know you before making plans that big.' Say it once. No apology attached.

steps.title: Watch the 48 hours after you pump the brakes
steps.desc: Give it two days after you slow things down. If they push back, pout, or disappear, the future-talk was pressure — not vision.

steps.title: Make one solo decision today
steps.desc: Choose something small — a night out alone, a solo weekend plan — and do it without asking. Note whether that's a problem for them.

cards.script: "I'm not there yet. Let's find out who we are first."
cards.counter:
When someone anchors you to a future fast, they make it hard to leave before you've had a chance to choose whether you want to stay.
• Notice: you start thinking of the relationship as 'already serious' without having decided it is.
• Say: 'I need more time before anything that size' — once, firmly.
• If they can't give you that, the pressure is the whole point.
cards.insight: The move that follows this one is guilt. Once you slow down the future-talk, they'll say you're not committed enough. That's the next card in their hand.

cards.title: The Gift That Creates a Debt
cards.hook: Extravagant gifts in week two aren't generosity. They're deposits into a debt you didn't agree to carry.
cards.truth:
Early gifts used for love bombing work by triggering your urge to give something back.
• Receiving something big makes you feel obligated — even if you never asked for it.
• The bomber knows this. The gift is for the obligation it creates, not for you.
• The trap: once you accept the first big gift, saying no to anything later feels ungrateful.
cards.remember: Gifts you didn't ask for are sometimes just unpaid bills.
cards.theySee: A new date who arrives with expensive gifts or pays for elaborate nights out, very early, before any real closeness exists.

signals.t: Gifts or dates are far more expensive than anything normal for the stage you're at together.
They give presents with no birthday, holiday, or milestone to explain them.
They bring up what they've done for you when you set a limit or push back on something.
After a conflict or your resistance, something extravagant appears and is expected to close the matter.

steps.title: Decline one gift today
steps.desc: When the next gift or grand gesture arrives, say: 'That's too much — I'm not comfortable taking that.' Watch the full reaction, not just the first response.

steps.title: Write what's been given
steps.desc: List everything they've done for you so far. Notice if the list is one-sided. Notice if they've mentioned any part of that list when you've pushed back on something.

steps.title: Track what follows friction
steps.desc: Every time you disagree or pull back in the next week, note whether a gift, dinner, or grand gesture appears within 24–48 hours afterward.

cards.script: "That's way too much for where we are. I don't want to take that."
cards.counter:
When someone's gifts make you feel obligated rather than happy, the gift is already working on you.
• Notice: you say yes to things you'd normally refuse, because of what they've given.
• Say: 'I need to make this decision on its own — not based on what you've done for me.'
• If they call that unfair, the gift was always a trade.
cards.insight: The bigger the gift, the harder it is to walk away without feeling like you owe something. That difficulty is the whole point of giving it.

cards.title: Cutting You Off From the People Who'd Warn You
cards.hook: They don't tell you to stop seeing your friends. They just make sure you'd rather see them — until seeing anyone else feels like a problem you'd have to manage.
cards.truth:
Isolation in love bombing is quiet. It works by making you choose, not by making demands.
• They schedule things when you'd normally be with others. They get visibly hurt when you go anyway.
• Your friends see the speed. They say something. The bomber calls your friends jealous or unsupportive.
• The trap: once your friends stop calling because you keep canceling, you're alone with the one person who controls what's normal.
cards.remember: The person pulling you away from warnings is usually the warning.
cards.theySee: A new partner who always seems to need them urgently on the exact nights they planned to see someone else.

signals.t: Every time you plan to see friends, something urgent or emotional comes up on their end.
They call your close friends toxic, negative, or jealous without having spent real time with them.
You come home from seeing someone else and they ask why you needed to go, or act visibly withdrawn.
The nights you skip plans with others, they make the evening especially good — the pattern teaches itself.

steps.title: Book a friends plan now
steps.desc: Set a date with one close friend for this week. Tell the new partner about it in advance. Do not cancel, whatever comes up.

steps.title: Ask your closest friend directly
steps.desc: Call one person who knew you before this relationship. Ask them: 'Have I seemed different? Have I been harder to reach?' Listen without defending the new partner.

steps.title: Count the cancellations
steps.desc: Look at the last 30 days. Add up every time you canceled something with someone else because of this person. If the number is more than two, write it down as a fact.

cards.counter:
When someone consistently makes you less available to the people who'd notice what's happening, the isolation is already working.
• Notice: you're defending the new partner to old friends more than you're talking about them warmly.
• Don't confront the partner yet — rebuild contact with one friend first, this week.
• If the partner reacts badly to that one rebuilt friendship, your friends were right.
cards.insight: The friends you pushed away during this period are the same ones who will tell you the truth when it's over. The question is whether you let it go long enough that they've stopped trying.

cards.title: Ignoring Your Limits to See What You'll Accept
cards.hook: The first time they cross a line and nothing happens, that becomes the new line. They're not being careless — they're reading you.
cards.truth:
Crossing your limits early is a test, not a mistake.
• Every limit they cross and get away with moves what's acceptable a little further forward.
• They watch how you react. A mild protest with no follow-through is a green light.
• The trap: by the time the violations feel serious, you've already accepted a hundred small ones.
cards.remember: Every ignored no teaches them exactly what they can do next.
cards.theySee: A new date who shows up unannounced, calls after being told not to, or keeps pushing a topic after you've said you're finished with it.

signals.t: They show up at your home or workplace without being invited, presented as a romantic surprise.
You say you're not ready for something and they raise it again two days later as if you never spoke.
You ask them to stop a behavior, they stop briefly, then it comes back within a week.
When called out, they apologize sincerely — then do the exact same thing again within days.

steps.title: Name one crossed line today
steps.desc: Pick one thing they did that you didn't like. Write it in plain words. Write what you said or didn't say afterward. Be exact.

steps.title: Set the same limit again with a result attached
steps.desc: Say what you need clearly and say what you will do if it happens again. Then actually do it if it happens.

steps.title: Track repeats for 7 days
steps.desc: Write down every time the same behavior shows up again after you've addressed it. More than once means the apologies were managing you, not changing anything.

cards.script: "I said no to that. If it happens again, I'm stepping back from this."
cards.counter:
If someone keeps crossing the same lines after you address them, ask yourself — are you enforcing anything, or just talking?
• Notice: the apologies feel genuine but the behavior keeps coming back.
• Say the limit one more time, with a real result attached that you will follow through on.
• If you don't follow through, you've confirmed the limit isn't real.
cards.insight: The violations stay small on purpose. Nothing is ever quite big enough to justify leaving — until it is. By then you've spent months saying things and doing nothing about them.

cards.title: Check the Clock: Healthy Relationships Don't Sprint
cards.hook: New things grow at a natural pace. When the pace feels dictated by one person and not by both of you, that's worth stopping on — today, not later.
cards.truth:
Speed is the bomber's core tool. It works by keeping you reacting instead of choosing.
• When things move fast, you don't have time to think. That's not a coincidence.
• Real closeness grows when both people set the pace. Love bombing has one driver.
• The trap: fast feels exciting. You confuse the speed with the feeling, and the feeling with love.
cards.remember: Real closeness comes from both people choosing it — not one person pushing.
cards.theySee: A new couple where one person is always two steps ahead — already declaring love or planning the future before the other has caught up.

signals.t: They've said 'I love you', planned the future, and told their family about you — before you've caught up to any of it.
There are no slow weeks. Every week has a new milestone they're pushing toward without asking if you're ready.
When you go slower, they say you're not invested, not serious, or not sure about them.
Within a month, their things are at your place or they're there every night, without a direct conversation about it.

steps.title: Name where you actually are
steps.desc: Write down where you are emotionally right now — not where they say you should be. Are you two actually in the same place, or are you always chasing their level?

steps.title: Say one real thing you need before going further
steps.desc: Tell them one specific thing you need before moving to the next level. Be exact. See if that's something they can give you without pressure.

steps.title: Compare to your last healthy relationship
steps.desc: Think about a past relationship that ended cleanly. At the same number of weeks in, where were you? Use that as a real reference point — not a rule, a check.

cards.script: "I'm not at that point yet and I'm not going to pretend I am."
cards.counter:
When someone calls your natural pace a character flaw, they're telling you their pace is not negotiable.
• Notice: you feel behind in a race you didn't agree to enter.
• Say: 'I move at my own speed. That's not changing.'
• If they turn your pace into a sign of low commitment, the pace pressure is the control.
cards.insight: The bomber moves fast because time gives you information. Slow the clock and watch what they do with the extra space. That's when you see who they are.

cards.title: They Need You to Need Them: The Reassurance Demand
cards.hook: A person who needs to hear you're committed every few hours isn't insecure. They're checking whether the hook is still in.
cards.truth:
Constant reassurance demands aren't about their anxiety — they're about your compliance.
• Each time you reassure them, you practice being responsible for their emotional state.
• Managing their feelings becomes your default job over weeks.
• The trap: when the relationship turns controlling, leaving feels like abandoning someone fragile.
cards.remember: When their feelings become your daily job, that's management — not love.
cards.theySee: A new partner who asks repeatedly throughout the day whether you still like them, miss them, or are still interested in being together.

signals.t: They ask if you still like them or want them every single day, unprompted, from early on.
They start small arguments and then measure how hard you work to fix things afterward.
When you go quiet for a few hours, multiple follow-up messages arrive asking if you're angry or okay.
When you don't reassure fast enough, they go distant or cold until you pursue them again.

steps.title: Stop reassuring automatically today
steps.desc: The next time they ask if you still want them, pause before responding. Ask yourself honestly: is this coming from genuine desire to say it, or from obligation to fix their mood?

steps.title: Name what you're noticing
steps.desc: Say: 'I've noticed you need a lot of reassurance. I want to understand that.' Then listen without rushing to make them feel better.

steps.title: Hold one silence on purpose
steps.desc: When they go tense or cold without clear reason, don't chase for six hours. Log what they do during the wait and how you feel about not chasing.

cards.script: "I'm not going to reassure you every few hours. When I say something, I mean it."
cards.counter:
If you feel responsible for someone's emotional stability within weeks of meeting them, you're already managing them.
• Notice: you feel anxious when they seem unhappy, even briefly and for no clear reason.
• Say: 'Your feelings are yours to handle. I can care without carrying them.'
• If they push back on that, you're seeing them at their most honest.
cards.insight: The fragility is often constructed. Once you stop carrying it, you'll see exactly how fragile they actually are — and it's usually much less than they've shown you.

cards.title: When They Pull Back: Anger and Withdrawal as Control
cards.hook: The bomber who flooded you with attention will also use its sudden removal to pull you back. The withdrawal is the other half of the same weapon.
cards.truth:
Hot-and-cold cycling works because your brain chases the warmth after the cold hits.
• The sudden coldness triggers real panic in someone who just had constant warmth. You scramble to fix it.
• When you chase, they warm back up. You learn: their warmth returns if you work for it.
• The trap: you're now trained to manage their moods to keep the relationship livable.
cards.remember: Going cold is a button press. Don't chase it.
cards.theySee: A partner who was warm and attentive for weeks, who suddenly becomes cold, distant, or quietly angry — with no explanation offered.

signals.t: They go from intense warmth to near silence within hours, with no clear trigger you can point to.
When you ask what's wrong, they say 'nothing' — but stay cold until you pursue harder.
The moment you slow down or create any distance, they express anger or hurt — not sadness, anger.
As soon as you reach out and work to fix things, their warmth comes back immediately as if nothing happened.

steps.title: Don't chase the next cold spell
steps.desc: When they go cold without explanation, wait 24 hours before reaching out. Write down how you feel during the wait — anxious, relieved, angry. That feeling is information.

steps.title: Name the pattern out loud
steps.desc: Say: 'I've noticed you go quiet when I slow down, and come back when I reach out. I need to understand what's happening there.'

steps.title: Decide your move before it happens again
steps.desc: Write one sentence right now — what you will do the next time they go cold without explanation. Make the decision before you're inside the feeling.

cards.script: "When you go quiet without telling me why, I don't chase. That's not something I do."
cards.counter:
If you're managing someone's moods to keep the warmth available, the cycle is already running on you.
• Notice: you feel relief when they're warm again — not just happy, but relieved, like a threat passed.
• Say nothing to them yet — count how many times the cycle runs in one week.
• One cold-and-warm is noise. Three is a system. Decide which you're in.
cards.insight: The person who controls warmth controls the relationship. Once you stop chasing the cold, you'll find out very quickly what's real and what was bait.

cards.title: The Slow-Test: Check What You're Actually Dealing With
cards.hook: You don't have to name what's happening yet. You just have to slow down and watch what they do with the space you create.
cards.truth:
Love bombing stops working when you stop feeding it with urgency and constant attention.
• A healthy person handles your pace and respects your space. The bomber escalates.
• The slow-test needs no confrontation. You just stop running at their speed.
• The trap to avoid: testing with cruelty or games. Go slow, not cold. Observe, don't punish.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 4 — Always Say Less Than Necessary
cards.remember: Slow down and watch who they become when you stop being easy.
cards.theySee: A partner who has been all-in from the start, noticing the other person becoming slightly less reactive and harder to read.

signals.t: You leave 3–4 hours between replies and multiple follow-ups arrive before you respond.
You say no to one plan and observe whether they accept it or make it into something to manage.
You say you need a night alone and watch whether they honor it without drama.
You push back on something minor and see whether they listen or immediately redirect back to their ask.

steps.title: Pick one area to slow down in today
steps.desc: Choose one behavior — reply speed, availability, how much you initiate — and cut it in half for five days. Don't explain it. Just observe.

steps.title: Log every response to the slowdown
steps.desc: Keep a running note of how they react to the change. How often? What emotion? Pressure and guilt are different from patience.

steps.title: Compare who they are now to week one
steps.desc: After five days, write two sentences: who they were in week one, and who they are now. If those are two different people, that's your answer.

cards.script: "I'm around, just been in my own head. I'll reach out when I'm ready."
cards.counter:
If you're on the receiving end of a slow-test, the right move is patience — not pressure.
• Notice: if you feel the urge to escalate or demand contact when someone slows down, examine that urge first.
• Say: 'Take the time you need. I'm here.'
• If you can't say that and mean it, check what you actually want from this.
cards.insight: The slow-test doesn't lie. The person who's fine with your pace is still there on day five. The bomber usually makes it clear by day two.

cards.title: When You Name It: What Comes Next
cards.hook: The moment you name what's been happening, the dynamic shifts fast. Know what's coming before you say it — because they'll have a move ready, and you need one too.
cards.truth:
Naming love bombing out loud usually gets one of two responses: rage or tears. Rarely calm.
• The bomber almost never goes quietly. They turn your clarity into cruelty, paranoia, or ingratitude.
• They may escalate — more gifts, bigger declarations — to pull you back before you go.
• The trap: their reaction to being named feels like proof you were wrong. It isn't.
cards.principle: Eddy: JADE Trap — Justify, Argue, Defend, Explain
cards.remember: Name it once, clearly. Their reaction tells you everything.
cards.theySee: A partner who has just told them they felt overwhelmed, pushed, or controlled — and is watching carefully for what comes next.

signals.t: They respond to your naming it with extreme emotion — either anger or collapse — not calm, measured words.
They turn your concern into an attack on them and make you the one who owes an apology.
They make one last grand gesture — biggest gift, biggest declaration — right after you name it.
They tell you you're paranoid, broken, or that no one else will treat you as well as they have.

steps.title: Say it once in plain words
steps.desc: Say what you saw, what it cost you, and what you need now. One clear statement per point. Not a list of grievances — specific, plain, short.

steps.title: Don't JADE — don't justify or defend
steps.desc: When they push back, resist explaining more. You've said it. Each additional explanation gives them another opening to argue you out of what you know.

steps.title: Have a plan for the 48 hours after
steps.desc: Before the conversation, decide where you'll be, who you'll call, and what you'll do if they escalate. Have one person's number ready to call that night.

cards.script: "What happened here moved too fast and felt like pressure. I'm stepping back to figure out what I actually want."
cards.counter:
If someone is naming this pattern at you, the only response that preserves anything is space — not argument.
• Notice: if your first instinct is to argue, cry, or chase — wait 24 hours before doing any of it.
• Say: 'I hear you. Take the time you need.' Then stop talking.
• If they named something real, no amount of explaining will undo it.
cards.insight: The person who can hear 'this was too much' without collapsing or attacking is the one worth talking to. Most won't be. Now you know which one you're dealing with.
